svg.font-family: Inter, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Supply firms up, and slips, in steps of its own
svg.desc: Two parts. At the top, demand's stages (Intent, Dated, Configured, Live, Organic) mirror supply's (planned, contracted, under construction, delivered, live), with both scored on promised against actual size and date by stage (mechanisms 2 and 11); a planner who discounts demand intents but takes supply promises at face value has half an outside view. Below, a chain: a late transformer delays the building, then every rack and turn-up committed on the old date, and the slipped batches queue at turn-up together, so a slip often shows up twice. Side notes: decommission is negative supply [2], so a slipped retirement can stall an on-time delivery; and four sites that wait on one transformer supplier or utility slip together. A footer says a supply slip is an envelope change in time, handled as a re-cut. Schematic.

text.tspan: Score both the same way: promised against actual
size and date, by stage (mechanisms 2 and 11)
intents but takes supply promises at
face value has half an outside view.

svg.text: so a slip often shows up twice (Section 6.2)

text.tspan: A retirement is a supply order with a minus sign: it has
a date, and it slips. Old racks must leave before new
ones can use their power and floor, so a slipped
decommission can stall a delivery that arrived on time.

svg.text: same transformer supplier, or same utility

text.tspan: Four sites with independent risks usually deliver most of what
was promised; four that wait on one supplier slip together.

svg.text: A supply slip is an envelope change in time, handled as a re-cut (Section 9.1).
